David Moyes took a glug of water and glanced up at the big screen away to his right, almost as if he wanted confirmation that what he was seeing was true.

Had he looked behind him, Moyes would have seen Andy Burnham and his wife, Marie-France, in raptures, along with thousands of others. It was true, all right. Everton had scored their third goal and were bounding into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, seemingly without a care in the world.

What a happy change of direction. Moyes has spent months spinning plates, dealing with owners who do not care about a proud club and want to sell up and a squad that was left criminally short in the transfer window. Then, before Newcastle’s visit, came more disruption.

Jack Grealish’s selfish and reckless decision to go Awol from training on Monday could have been a catalyst for more misery and invited Newcastle to deliver a hammer blow to Everton’s season, but again, Moyes fostered a siege mentality. He was rewarded in the most emphatic fashion.

True, Newcastle collapsed like a deckchair without hinges and this performance – which encouraged many of their 8,000 followers to head for the exits early – would not have done anything to convince those who view Matthias Jaissle, the head coach, with ambivalence to change their minds.

The lack of discipline in their ranks was exposed when Dan Burn scored a late consolation and ended up in a melee with James Tarkowski and Joelinton. But the issues Jaissle, who lamented that “we must improve”, has to correct are for another day: this contest belonged to Everton.

Thierno Barry had provided the finish that secured a trip to Fleetwood in December and what an opportunity it is for Moyes to make Everton semi-finalists in this competition for the first time since 2016. Whether Grealish will have a part to play in it remains to be seen.

Thierno Barry with Everton's third! 🔵 https://t.co/dyb8fKud8N

The last thing Everton needed on a night of such importance was a distraction. Grealish will have a tough job mending relations, particularly with Moyes, but there was a paradox: though he had caused a major issue for 90 minutes he became an irrelevance.

Moyes is impatient to give Evertonians a big day out and his only focus was on crossing this hurdle – for all that Newcastle have had a turbulent start to the campaign, they are dangerous opponents and you wondered in the fraught opening 30 minutes if they might exacerbate the hosts’ woes.

As Jaissle hopped and squirmed on the sidelines, imploring Newcastle forward, chances came and went: Harvey Barnes had a header saved, Fabian Schar tested Jordan Pickford from 30 yards while Vitalii Mykolenko and James Tarkowski made huge goal-saving challenges.

“We should have scored more goals,” Jaissle, who was dressed as if auditioning for the role of The Milk Tray Man, growled. “It [losing] was shocking as the game was not that bad.”

Moyes was infuriated by Everton’s initial inertia, so much so there was a point when the Scot prevented Merlin Röhl, his own full-back, from taking a throw-in until Tarkowski and Jake O’Brien had complied with his gesturing to get 10 yards further forward.

It might have looked old-fashioned but it worked. Suddenly Everton started asking questions, Hayden Hackney almost got on the end of a cross from Mykolenko, and it encouraged the supporters on the vertiginous South Stand to raise their voices and become more involved.

What they needed was a goal to set things alight and in the 34th minute, it arrived. Tyrique George won possession by Newcastle’s corner flag, the ball dropped at Hackney’s feet and he instinctively ushered it on to James Garner, who whipped a right-footed drive beyond Lukáš Horníček.

James Garner puts Everton in front against Newcastle in the Carabao Cup! 🔵 https://t.co/TzponbWyGU

The roar that greeted it was a mix of elation and wonder, relief and desperation. The locals have grown weary of seeing nights with potential end in disappointment but here was the foothold they craved and the opportunity they were ready to seize. Soon the lead would be doubled.

Hackney would score the goal, converting a super Barry cross, but let us acknowledge the fabulous refereeing of Farai Hallam, who waved play on when he might have whistled for a foul on Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. And how Everton took advantage.

Hayden Hackney doubles Everton's advantage! 🔵 https://t.co/VIY0Iln3nI

It must be said the officiating this week has, in the main, been outstanding. Watching a match without the persistent spectre of VAR has been liberating and you can see the referees have felt free to make decisions on instinct.

The whole experience of knowing a contest cannot be re-refereed has been better for all. It will not catch on, sadly, because too many people have gone too far down the road with VAR, but we should embrace the purity of “old school football” while we can.

Evertonians – the Prime Minister included – certainly embraced the buffer of a second goal and the fact Hackney scored it also felt like a throwback: a player who was plucked out of the Championship in the summer and encouraged by Moyes to show he could make the next step up.

He did that and so, too, did Everton, their progress was assured in the 69th minute when Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall dashed down the left and crossed for Barry to finish. Moyes puffed out his cheeks as it hit the net. He, more than most, deserved to enjoy this one.

#1152. NWSL Decision Day storylines: Gotham, San Diego Wave chase Shield, last playoff spots up for grabs

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There may still be a regular-season weekend left on the NWSL calendar, but for a few of the league's teams, Sunday's fixtures will see them slip into postseason mode a week in advance with plenty on the line on Decision Day.

The main characters will be Gotham FC and the Seattle Reign, each in control of their fate with different tasks ahead. Gotham have a chance to win the NWSL Shield for the very first time in Sunday's clash against the Utah Royals, with inconsistency in the final months of the season pushing the race for the trophy to the last day of the regular season. They are favored to collect the prize but have a formidable foe in the San Diego Wave, whose chances took a hit with last week's draw against the Boston Legacy.

The Reign, meanwhile, face the Orlando Pride in a game they must win to secure a spot in the playoffs. The North Carolina Courage are just two points behind them, and the Denver Summit three, with those two facing off against each other in the hope that the Reign slip up and hand one of them the chance to overtake.

Here's a look at what's to come as the NWSL regular season comes to a close.

Gotham have been favored to win the NWSL Shield for months, to the point that they had a seven-point lead in late summer. Even in a stretch of late-season ups and downs, though, their grip on first place has loosened but never slipped, leaving them well placed to win the trophy for the first time on Sunday. They boast a three-point lead over the Wave on Decision Day, a draw against the Royals enough to clinch the Shield, no matter what happens in the Wave's trip to Bay FC.

The bigger question for Gotham, though, is whether or not they will be at full strength a week before the playoffs begin. Jaedyn Shaw and Rose Lavelle both missed last week's 2-1 win at the Pride, while Shaw was also an unused substitute in a 1-0 loss at the Washington Spirit a week earlier. The pair have been Gotham's most impactful attackers this season, racking up a combined 22 goal contributions along the way; Shaw in particular has been both a goalscoring threat and a creative outlet, so much so that Gotham's attacking output fades considerably when she's not on the pitch. The league leaders might survive Sunday's clash without the U.S. women's national team standouts, the playoff-bound Royals set to enter the postseason with a middling defensive record.

Seven of the eight playoff spots are already booked, with three teams now vying for the final berth, and the margins will be tight for each of them. The Seattle Reign currently sit in eighth with 42 points, a win over the Pride enough to seal the deal. If they slip up, there are two teams in the waiting -- the North Carolina Courage and the Denver Summit, who play each other on Sunday. The Courage need to win and hope the Reign drop points to land in the top eight, while the Summit need to win plus a Reign loss to make the playoffs in their inaugural season.

There's a layer of unpredictability naturally baked into the scenario. The Reign not only have the easiest path -- win and they're in -- but they face a team whose playoff hopes were dashed some time ago. Their defense has really propped them up, conceding just 33 goals despite posting 39.96 expected goals against this season. Their rivals have their own strengths, the Summit finding form thanks to Lindsey Heaps' seven goals and three assists since her midseason arrival. The Courage, meanwhile, have this season's cheat code in Ashley Sanchez and speaking of...

With 20 goals this season, Sanchez's MVP argument writes itself at this point, but she has a chance to bolster her campaign on Sunday and make history along the way. She would set the NWSL's single-season goalscoring record if she scores against the Summit, while that goal or an assist would allow her to break Temwa Chawinga's single-season goal contributions record. It would be a worthy reward for Sanchez, whose conversion to left wing this season has been transformational and resulted in a well-earned return to the national team, thrusting her fully into the conversation for a spot on next summer's Women's World Cup roster. It is almost inconceivable, then, that her powers alone will not at least guarantee the Courage a spot in the postseason. Then again, they have maybe been overly reliant on Sanchez's form, the winger contributing to nearly half of the team's goals this campaign. They have been sunk, though, by a leaky defense, the Courage ranking in the league's bottom six for goals conceded. Missing the playoffs is unlikely to jeopardize Sanchez's MVP case, but it will speak to the Courage's limitations if they cannot sneak above the playoff line on the final day of the regular season.

#1149. Dejected Dimitar Berbatov has his head in his hands as he realises Man United are now in relegation zone - but admits old side DESERVE to be there

Published: 18:52 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 20:33 EDT, 7 November 2026

Former Manchester United legend Dimitar Berbatov has blasted his old side, saying they deserve to be in the relegation zone.

United plunged into the bottom three on Saturday afternoon, perversely as neighbours Manchester City lost 3-1 away to Nottingham Forest.

The Bulgarian looked devastated when he was informed of United’s predicament while working on beIN Sports' coverage of the City game but still sounded hopeful that United could turn their form around.

When his attention was drawn to the Premier League table, the two-time Premier League winner initially had his head in his hands before saying: 'I don't believe it, but the way United are playing sometimes they deserve to be there honestly.'

Berbatov then took up a more positive tune saying: ‘Tomorrow they still have a game.'

United host Aston Villa on Sunday and after winning against Roma in midweek have the perfect opportunity finally to end their seven-game winless run in the league.

Berbatov could barely look at the table after United plunged into the drop zone

Berbatov won five major trophies as well as Premier League golden boot in four years at Manhchetser United

The fixture could prove either to be the nail in the coffin for United manager Michael Carrick or afford him more time after a woeful start to the season.

Berbatov won his two Premier Leagues alongside Carrick and will hope his ex-colleague can find a way to keep his job.

If he fails to guide his team to a victory against Villa it could be bleak for Carrick, as he has not been given any guarantees over his future beyond Sunday's game against Aston Villa.

Club chiefs handed Carrick more time to turn the club's season around following the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth a fortnight ago amid speculation he could be replaced by Eddie Howe or Julian Nagelsmann.

In the two games since then, Carrick's side have lost at Chelsea and staged a rousing comeback over Roma in the Champions League to secure a first win in ten games.

But now the onus is on Carrick to build on the momentum gained from their Champions League victory.

When the final whistle sounded, it was Gotham FC that lifted the NWSL Shield, with San Diego Wave finishing just behind in second place, and Seattle Reign grabbing the final playoff spot.

Here are the big takeaways from the chaotic day:

Gotham FC 2, Utah Royals 0 San Diego Wave 1, Bay FC 0Kansas City Current 2, Racing Louisville 0 Washington Spirit 2, Chicago Stars 0 Seattle Reign 1, Orlando Pride 0Angel City 4, Boston Legacy 1 North Carolina Courage 1, Denver Summit 0 Portland Thorns 2, Houston Dash 0

With decision day done and dusted, the final results confirm the 2026 NWSL playoff bracket. More decision-day wins by Washington Spirit, 2-0 over Chicago, and Kansas City Current's 2-0 win against Racing Louisville confirm they get to host at least one home playoff game. First-place Gotham and second-place San Diego will also host, and if they win in the quarters, they will host semifinal fixtures.

San Diego, Angel City, and Kansas City all step into the playoffs on hot streaks. All three clubs are unbeaten in their last five games, with the Current on a five-game win streak.

Gotham needed only a draw to clinch their first-ever Shield in club history, but they did more than that and won 2-0 at home at Sports Illustrated Stadium. The club heads into the playoffs as the top seed after winning previous NWSL Championships as the lowest-ranked eighth seed.

The East Coast side has been a force to be reckoned with, winning the Shield during the longest season ever, the league's first 30-match schedule. The club had a significant points margin in late summer, but inconsistency and roster rotation due to injuries down the stretch pushed the Shield race to decision day, with Washington Spirit in contention through the penultimate matchweek and San Diego Wave still in contention on decision day.

San Diego did their part to make things interesting with a 1-0 win at Bay FC, but Gotham's early attacking surge set them up for success. Forward Midge Purce created the space for a laser cross in front of goal to Guro Reiten.

The lengthy season has affected all clubs this year, though Gotham's late-season string of injuries was particularly noticeable, with recent season-ending injuries to defender Bruninha and breakout rookie forward Jordynn Dudley. She's rocking a leg sleeve now and making an impact for the club, and scored the last goal after subbing in.

THAT’S JUST HOW IT’S DONE pic.twitter.com/BEj9KsAu6p

The goal sealed the win, and the return of Shaw and Rose Lavelle, both from injury, was a welcome sight for a team that has leaned on depth all season. Midfielder Jaelin Howell, among the team leaders in minutes played, left the match in the first half with a right ankle injury and will be evaluated closer to the quarterfinals. For now, Gotham capped the race that was theirs to win.

The eighth and final NWSL playoff spot came down to a battle between three clubs. Seattle Reign controlled their own fate, while North Carolina Courage and Denver Summit each needed to take the other out and root for Orlando Pride to win.

Seattle's identity this year has been more about organization and defense than goals, and their 1-0 victory over Orlando to clinch the final playoff spot was about as representative of the 2026 Seattle Reign as you could get. Playing particularly motivated, with playoffs at stake, and honoring longtime Reign veteran Jess Fishlock, Seattle pulled ahead just past the hour mark on a set piece that featured not one, but two flicks, and a clinical finish by center back Jordyn Bugg.

#1143. Clearing the way for a transformative stem-cell treatment for Parkinson’s disease

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Joohi Jimenez-Shahed studies movement disorders, neuromodulation and brain circuit therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City.

Big improvements in Parkinson’s disease treatment have been few and far between. The tantalizing prospect of regenerative stem-cell therapies to address this neurodegenerative condition is therefore creating considerable excitement.

A core component of Parkinson’s is the loss of dopamine-producing neurons, which normally provide carefully controlled neurotransmitter signals to the brain’s movement circuits1. This leads to people having substantial difficulties performing routine activities.

A dopamine-replacement approach provided one of the first major advances in Parkinson’s treatment2. Levodopa, a chemical precursor to dopamine that was introduced in the 1960s, treats symptoms effectively. But the levodopa honeymoon can be short. As the effect duration of each dose wanes, extra doses or medications are required to keep dopamine levels from falling. And the drug can come with a complication that many patients dread — writhing, uncontrolled involuntary movements known as dyskinesia. A surgical approach called deep brain stimulation (DBS) can mitigate these complications effectively3.

The downsides of levodopa raise a question: rather than replacing dopamine, why not replace the cellular machinery that produces it? Enter the dopaminergic stem cell. Engineered from cells sampled from an adult’s own tissues (known as autologous) or from a different individual (allogeneic), induced-pluripotent stem cells can be safely transplanted into human brains and can improve movement-related Parkinson’s symptoms, such as tremors, stiffness and slowness, without worsening dyskinesia4.

Only a few dozen people have received this experimental treatment. Major brain surgery is required to transplant the cells. Allogeneic cell transplants also require recipients to undertake a year of immunosuppression to ensure that the cells survive. Autologous cell transplants avoid this, but it takes 6–8 months to produce the cells for each patient.

It is not yet known how cell therapies will measure up to current standards of care. Early studies have been in people with advanced disease. At this stage, the chance of benefit might be reduced: the cells are implanted into an already degenerating circuit that could be difficult to restore.

Critics might therefore argue that dopamine cell therapies cannot produce a more robust effect than levodopa or DBS without imposing excess cost or risk. But the way that Parkinson’s treatments are investigated and approved can neither fully support this pessimistic view nor provide sufficient evidence for a more optimistic one.

Therapeutic development for Parkinson’s has mainly aimed to relieve symptoms. A more ambitious goal would be to slow the disease’s progression by altering its underlying biology. Yet there are substantial obstacles to developing such a treatment.

Implicit to the concept of disease modification is the need for a biomarker that measures the underlying biological processes5. Although a biological definition of Parkinson’s is emerging, it applies mainly to the identification of early disease. Relatively little is known about how such markers evolve in Parkinson’s, or how they relate to clinical progression6.

Long-term, multi-site observational studies such as the Parkinson’s Precision Medicine Initiative (see go.nature.com/4ayapbI) provide an ideal framework for exploring digital, biological and imaging markers, while benchmarking disease progression. Their success depends on building and sustaining large consortia, and on a healthy dose of time and effort from researchers and study participants, but the studies are constrained by funding inequities.

Even if such biomarkers were already at researchers’ disposal, there is no specific guidance from the US Food and Drug Administration on developing disease-modifying treatments7. The agency’s Regenerative Medicine Advanced Therapy designation speeds up cell- and gene-therapy development and approval. But eligibility requires only the intent to treat, modify, reverse or cure a serious disorder. As a result, clinical trials of regenerative therapies are likely to be designed to show benefits to a person’s symptoms without incurring the added cost and burden of showing a change in biology — a pragmatic but less ambitious path.

Crucially, supportive evidence for the broader potential of dopaminergic cell therapies is what will define their advantage. Cell dose, optimal treatment timing and objective evidence of cell survival, engraftment and effects on brain-network function would demonstrate whether cell therapies can produce lasting change in people with Parkinson’s. Public–private research partnerships could refine the required measurement tools and generate such data.

The ability to transform stem cells into dopamine-producing neurons and transplant them safely into human brains is momentous. Its use as a treatment extends an opportunity to chart another course for people with Parkinson’s by limiting levodopa complications and possibly the need for DBS. This outcome would bolster the hopes of people with this condition. But the real therapeutic breakthrough will occur only when scientists and regulators converge to advance the goal of restoring neural circuitry and function. That would be a truly bold step towards conquering this this relentless disease.

#1140. Kai Havertz's offside problem: Arsenal star has been caught astray FIFTEEN times already this season - and even Mikel Arteta admits striker must address his issue - as imperious defence bails champions out again

Published: 02:00 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 02:26 EDT, 8 November 2026

There’s being eager to break through on goal — and then there is Kai Havertz.

Aside from squandered chances, the sight of the Arsenal striker being caught offside at some point in a match this season is an expectation.

Havertz has been penalised for offside 15 times in the Premier League this season, which is seven times more than Leeds striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin (in 2nd on eight offsides).

Last season, Bukayo Saka was caught offside 14 times in the league. It is not good enough, and an issue which must be rectified.

A wider scoreline, fronted by Havertz taking his chances, would often change the trajectory of Arsenal matches. Certainly, the 1-0 victory against Hull City on Saturday didn’t need to be so tight.

Mikel Arteta, who can often be defensive of scrutinised players, didn’t even try to mask Havertz’s offside problem afterwards.

Kai Havertz has an issue with repeatedly being caught offside and Mikel Arteta knows he must improve that aspect of his game when leading the line

He said: ‘Yes, it’s something to improve. That's related sometimes to the timing (of the delivery) or really the situation, or the position, where he's lined up and what space he's given. But certainly it's far too many (offsides).

‘I think the sample is quite short to analyse it, but you have a point there. It's a combination. It's all about timing. So there is a signal on the ball, and you need to time it around that.’

A number of deliveries into the final third saw the striker caught out for getting too excited and breaching the backline too early.

The most crucial stray offside against Hull was on the stroke of half-time, Martin Odegaard’s pass aimed in the path of Havertz. As he reached for the ball, Nobel Mendy had grabbed the German’s shirt, tugging him back. A VAR check resulted in referee Farai Hallam announcing that the shirt pull was a foul — but Havertz was offside, meaning no penalty.

It’s a more complex situation, though, than the German simply being too eager in latching onto deliveries.

His team-mates are, on occasion, guilty of not passing to Havertz more sooner. Instead of playing the ball as soon as the opportunity opens up, the delay causes the forward to second-guess himself on when to break ahead.

So the onus is on the Arsenal midfield to time their through balls better, and better understand Havertz’s patterns of play, too. If both elements can click, Havertz and Arsenal’s goal tally will see an uptick.

Otherwise, only the striker’s offside infringement tally will continue to be the beneficiary.

Havertz will latch onto more chances if he is played in at the right time by midfielders

A 1-0 to the Arsenal pattern is already emerging.

Saturday’s victory over Hull was the Gunners’ fifth by such a scoreline across all competitions this season.

The ability to edge matches is a necessary ingredient in a title-winning campaign, particularly in sub-optimal performances.

The Gunners were seriously wasteful in their chances, which better sides will punish. Yet, it’s their ability to carry out wave upon wave of attack, almost expecting the sheer pressure to eventually produce a goal, that is ultimately hard for opponents to resist.

Overall, it’s the north London club’s equal-best start to a league season: 27 points from 10 games, equalling the same tally from their 2022-23 campaign. Their title defence is on the right track — according to the points tallies, anyway.

Arsenal's defence has been integral to their success this season and kept another clean sheet

The Hull City blueprint is a plan other underdog sides should assess when facing Arsenal.

The so-called ‘park the bus’ defensive set-ups are a commonality at the Emirates, owing to the calibre of players both in Arsenal’s starting XI and on their bench.

If a team survives the initial onslaught by the hour mark, Arteta typically turns to the bench and breaks a game open with a change or three.

Here, Piero Hincapie, Mikel Merino, Viktor Gyokeres and Eberechi Eze all came on before 70 minutes, their fresh legs helping breakdown Hull’s stubborn defence.

Still, the visitors’ high backline is a shrewd set-up which did work to great effect - before Odegaard’s strike.

Arsenal expect inferior sides to sit back, soak up the pressure and mount the odd counter-attack.

By pushing defenders higher up the pitch, it forced Arteta to adapt his carefully laid plans and gave his players a different dimension to navigate, slightly throwing them off track. Manager Sergej Jakirovic deserves his credit.

Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic came up with an excellent strategy that other sides could use

The final word must go to Noni Madueke. He’s received his fair share of scrutiny this season, the winger’s end product an area which is continually brought up.

When in full flow, he is so hard to stop because of his quick feet and directness — which is why more is often expected of Madueke. He is some talent.

Eze, on the bench, was called up by Thomas Tuchel for his latest England squad, with Madueke left out.

On the basis of this, and other recent performances, Madueke has been hard done by.

Though, with Saka sidelined, he can use the next two weeks to ready himself for some huge Arsenal games ahead against Borussia Dortmund, Manchester City and Real Madrid. The opportunity to stake a real claim in Arteta’s side is there for the taking.

#1138. Man Utd the masters of self-destruction as pressure piles on Carrick

So where do Manchester United go from here? It is never a good look when opposition fans start willing a rival club to stick with their manager, but that was the ignominy that had befallen Michael Carrick by the end of an afternoon in which Lisandro Martinez’s latest plastic hardman impression embodied the very worst of United’s self-sabotage.

After seeing their team go 2-0 up when Cole Palmer converted the penalty given away by Martinez’s lunacy, the Chelsea fans taunted Carrick with chants of “You’re getting sacked in the morning” and later “You’re going down with the City”, a nod to the other Manchester club who are crisis torn for very different reasons.

As the final whistle loomed, though, and with United just grateful Estevao had not punished Martinez’s red card more severely, the Chelsea fans had changed their tune. “Michael Carrick, we want you to stay,” came the chant from the Matthew Harding Stand and that cut far deeper.

And to think that the opening 45 minutes had offered United and their fans some hope of a little respite from the storm before ultimately giving way to an ever-darkening gloom.

Carrick, who had been given a stay of execution in midweek, said he still expected to be in charge for Roma’s visit to Old Trafford on Tuesday in the Champions League. But it is hard to escape the feeling that another managerial change will be coming at United before too long even if no one can be sure what happens next.

Equally, the prospect of more upheaval in the dugout might elicit little more than a shrug from fans pointing the finger squarely at the ownership and the executives they have appointed. The players were spared this time but Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers remained the target of sustained abuse as did Jason Wilcox, the director of football.

Defeat here extended United’s winless run to nine matches, their worst sequence for 38 years. They have taken just four points from the last 21 on offer in the Premier League and seem to be sinking fast. Carrick was asked about the team becoming mired in a relegation battle. This is the territory United are in.

The strange thing is this could and probably should have been a day when they at least stopped the rot for a few days. But more non-existent defending and brainlessness from Martinez, who was sent off for planting an elbow in Wesley Fofana’s face, put paid to that in a second half in which Carrick admitted United “unravelled”.

Chelsea were cut open on at least five occasions in a see-saw first half and Matheus Cunha also had a goal disallowed for a narrow offside. Xabi Alonso’s side had opportunities of their own – you will always get them against this United team – but they were second best and lucky not to be behind. Everyone talks about United being there for the taking, but the truth is Chelsea, coming off the back of a miserable defeat to Spurs and Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, were here.

The problem is Carrick’s team could not hit a barn door at the moment. They have scored just three goals in their last six league games and that lack of cutting edge was evident in the way Bruno Fernandes, back in the team as captain, and Amad Diallo (dangerous but with no end product) wasted excellent chances. That wastefulness would put pressure on any back line, let alone one with all the fortitude of wet cardboard. Chelsea were spared and exploited it with the help of the second and most corrosive acts of United’s self-mutilation.

We will come to Martinez’s sending off in a moment, but there had already been a cowardly act of a different kind from the Argentine defender before then in the lead-up to Chelsea’s opening goal soon after the restart.

Take nothing away from Morgan Rogers – his 40yd dash from the edge of the centre circle in United’s half to the six-yard box and the finish that followed were top notch. But where was the challenge? How could not a single player in red have stood in his path? “Come on Morgan, run through us buddy” seemed to be the message.

There were shades of the manner in which Rayan ran past him a week earlier in Bournemouth’s 3-0 win at Old Trafford. Rayan missed the chance but Rogers did no such thing, dinking the ball over Senne Lammens.

By the end, with Estevao – making the most of a first league start of the season – running riot and Chelsea smelling blood, Carrick would have been relieved the scoreline was not worse. Michael Carrick said he expects to be in charge of Manchester United next week despite Lisandro Martinez’s moment of madness leaving the club mired in a relegation battle and on their worst run for 38 years.

United were urged to sell Martinez after the controversial Argentina defender was sent off for elbowing Wesley Fofana as Carrick accused his side of “unravelling” as they slumped to a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea.

It left United without a win in nine matches, their worst run since 1988, and at risk of being sucked into the relegation zone. They have won just two of 13 games this season.

The Old Trafford hierarchy gave Carrick a stay of execution in midweek and, when asked if he expected to still to be at the helm when United face Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday, the head coach replied: “Yes. I’m just looking forward to getting the boys ready for midweek now.”

Having been booked moments earlier for a foul on Morgan Rogers, Martinez was sent off for a second yellow. The incident came less than three weeks after the Argentinian was fined and publicly apologised for attacking United director of football Jason Wilcox and the board over transfer policy and was the latest in a series of mistakes from him on the pitch this season.

Joe Cole, the former Chelsea and England forward, believes United must get rid of Martinez.

“Whatever the next Manchester United looks like, Lisandro Martinez has run his course,’ Cole said on TNT Sports. “He’s at the scene of the crime too often for Manchester United and is at fault for moments and goals like that. So that’s probably his time done.”

Carrick refused to publicly criticise Martinez but admitted his dismissal was a “huge moment” and felt his team “unravelled” in the second period.

“Things have gone against us in a big way,” the United manager said. “It’s unravelled quickly. There’s a lot of emotion right now. It’s a huge moment in the game. Asked if there would be a stigma attached to United potentially dropping into the relegation zone, Carrick added: “Not for me, no.”

And when asked how his players would deal with a relegation battle, Carrick added: “We’ve got to keep moving forward and winning games. There’s no words I’m going to explain to you now that makes any difference, it’s not going to change it. We’ve got to move forward and win matches.”

Good morning and welcome to live coverage of the Premier League match between Chelsea, who start the day in fifth, and 16th-placed Manchester United at Stamford Bridge. On Sunday and Monday it seemed certain that Michael Carrick would be relieved of his duties before today’s game but has survived for now, hoping to turn things around in the no man’s land that sometimes resembles a vote of confidence and at others a stay of execution.

Thirty years ago when Newcastle United were coming off the bridle in the title race with Manchester United, Alex Ferguson, as he then was, accused a Leeds team, who had been in freefall since the new year, of professional malpractice when they put in a rare display of passionate commitment and tenacity at Old Trafford in a 1-0 defeat.

“Why are they not in the top six?” asked Ferguson. “To me they’re cheating their manager. You wait and see the difference when they play Newcastle.” The hate between the Leeds and Manchester united fanbases was such, he implied, that they had decided to put a shift in because, for once, they feared the consequences if they had not. It seems to this observer that the boot is now on the other foot. These Manchester United players roused themselves to fight at Elland Road then chucked it in against Como and Bournemouth. If that’s not “cheating their manager”, what is?

Carrick will have to hope that some of the old hostility between Chelsea and Manchester United might encourage the players to run about a bit this afternoon and, at the very least, get stuck in rather than crumple spinelessly as they did last week. I doubt it would be enough to save Carrick’s job in the medium term but at least it would address whether they could stake a claim to be part of the rebuilding process.

As for Chelsea, who were awful in defeat by Brentford and Spurs either side of impressive victories over Bournemouth and at Everton, they need to find some defensive solidity, discipline and a way of terrorising defences in the absence of Joao Pedro. They are a work in progress still, in the fifth year of the hedge fund hegemony. For all that attacking talent and Moises Caicedo’s ability to steamroll midfielders, their defence does not inspire confidence and last year’s petulance continues to simmer.

#1136. What to watch in UEFA Champions League: Michael Carrick's Manchester United future on the line

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The midway point of the Champions League phase is upon us, and already the pressure is beginning to build on some of the biggest clubs in Europe. For some -- the likes of Bayern Munich, Inter and Manchester City -- the coming days will be about scrabbling back up the table and establishing a grip on one of the coveted top eight berths.

Altogether more significant are those teams who might have to legitimately worry about whether they can reach the top 24. On current form Manchester United are certainly among them, and their home game against Roma threatens to be critical for the club's Champions League prospects. Perhaps the future of their manager too.

A little over a week ago it seemed only logical to log the remainder of Michael Carrick's time as Manchester United manager in hours. Back-to-back defeats to Como and Bournemouth, each by a three-goal margin, had the club hovering around the drop zone in both the Premier League and Champions League standings. Club captain Bruno Fernandes had openly questioned Carrick's tactics, fostering a greater sense of mutiny in the aftermath of center back Lisandro Martinez turning both barrels on those in charge of appointing the manager and signing players. Remarkably, Carrick endured, part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the rest of the hierarchy concluding that the manager, who had led United to third last season, deserved time to right this listing ship. In many ways, events on Saturday vindicated that assessment. At Stamford Bridge the Red Devils had much the better of the first half, a coiled spring ready to blitz Chelsea on the counter. The only slight problem, one obviously out of Carrick's control, was that they did not put the ball in the net. Then the United midfield whooshed open like the doors of the Starship Enterprise to let Morgan Rogers score the opener, and everything adequate was undone in a 14-minute, Lisandro Martinez-authored head loss.

You can't really hold the manager responsible for that, not when so many coaches have tried and failed to quell United's appetite for self-destruction. Then again, it's not like you can sack the players midway through the season. If the situation gets perilous, there's not much you can do but start afresh in the dugout and hope against reason that Eddie Howe (or whoever else) can get through to this squad in a way his predecessors couldn't.

Right now you'd doubt that Manchester United are on the cusp of existential peril -- relegation to the Championship seems a long shot -- but they are at risk of being a few million worse off from their European campaign. Lose at home to Roma and they would have three points with half the league phase played. Still to play: Sporting and Villarreal away, RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich at home. That makes for a critical occasion against Roma, whose free-scoring attack must have been licking their lips on Saturday lunchtime. This has the makings of a brutal ending to a tenure that started with such promise.

Carrick sees things differently. "Perception is a funny thing," he said on Monday, insisting he does not feel like a coach with two games left to save his job. "You can make things look different ways and think about all sorts of different things. The commitment of the players to the club, to me, to each other - do not question at all. We need to play better, we can make better decisions, but the commitment is not a thing at all."

And yet, much as Carrick's perception of the group might quickly change, so could the game's view of why the United hierarchy stood by its man a week ago. Was the manager afforded faith for the long-term job or did his employers just conclude there was no sense in rushing a change ahead of a tricky three-game run before the international break? Fail to beat Roma and Aston Villa and we will surely find out.

Even in the aftermath of a derby defeat on Halloween night, it did not seem there was much cause for doom and gloom among the Inter ranks. A three-point deficit to league leaders Lazio is surely retrievable for the defending champions, and while they have only three points from their first three games, winning a man down against Shakhtar Donetsk eased any lingering sense of crisis about Champions League progression.

And yet the mood music emanating from the blue-and-black half of the San Siro paints a far more worrying picture. Head coach Cristian Chivu questioned the "approach and determination" of his side, senior center back Alessandro Bastoni spoke of an "inadequate" mentality and Nicolo Barella was the most damning of the lot. "We haven't had the right attitude since the start of the season, and it's a negative thing," he said, framing his side's struggles as being against tiredness as much as their opponents.

All of which might be something of an overreaction to Milan scoring three goals from five shots worth 0.57 expected goals in the first half at the weekend. Are there deep-seated problems with Inter or is this a team missing a host of senior players, among them Lautaro Martinez, whose absence at the weekend prompted Chivu to unsuccessfully experiment with Marcus Thuram as a lone striker?

Martinez will be missing for the trip to Feyenoord, but even without the captain, Bastoni, John Stones and Curtis Jones, there is the requisite quality in the Inter ranks to win well in Rotterdam (particularly if Chivu brings Federico Dimarco back into the XI). Whatever their attitude might be, it has not stopped them running up a supremely impressive 2.5 non-penalty expected goals per game. As for Europe, it would not have taken that many bounces going in a different direction for this team to have seven-plus points and be thinking about a return to the last 16. Without wishing to go too Leslie Nielsen about this, there really is nothing to see here.

Equally, when your players and coaches start talking in such apocalyptic terms, it is much more likely to bring on, well, the apocalypse. Or at least its Champions League league phase equivalent of an unseeded berth in the knockout playoffs/punishment round. That and some dropped points against Como and Atalanta.

Last time out we suggested that Arsenal's depth might hold the key against Bayern Munich late on and, like the stopped clock this column is, we were vindicated as Viktor Gyokeres turned provider for Declan Rice's late winner. Ultimately in the closing stages all Vincent Kompany had to turn to off the bench to aid his attack was a banged-up Luis Diaz and a faltering youngster in Lennart Karl. A fortnight later, even that would be an upgrade on the situation Bayern find themselves in as they travel to Madrid.

Saturday's 2-2 draw with Borussia Dortmund came at the cost of Ismael Saibari and Serge Gnabry, both of whom will be missing for some time yet. Jamal Musiala is also on the sidelines with a thigh injury and Diaz has only just returned to the field as he steps up his recovery from a hamstring injury. The best-case scenario for Bayern is that Michael Olise, who also exited early at the weekend, is able to play in some capacity, but director of sport Max Eberl described the Frenchman's situation as "day to day".

If Olise is not fit, it may be that the three attacking midfielders are Karl and two left backs, Alphonso Davies and Nathan Brown. It would take quite the center forward to knit all that together. A Ballon d'Or winner. Harry Kane's headline contribution to Der Klassiker might have been the missed penalty at 1-0, but the No. 9 ended this game with an assist for Dayot Upamecano and 0.43 expected assists total. Remarkably for a center forward, that was not even that far ahead of his season average of 0.32. That's 97th percentile for creation. It will not surprise you to know he ranks in the 99th percentile for shots and xG.

As Arsenal discovered to their cost in the last round of Champions League games, you can take away Kane's shooting chances, you can even take away his elite supporting cast, but he might still find a way to lay one on a plate for a teammate.

#1132. Inside Cristiano Ronaldo Jr's bid to step out of his father's shadow after his Portugal Under-17s call-up: From padel beef with Rio Ferdinand to a Coca-Cola BAN

Published: 02:00 EDT, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 02:46 EDT, 8 November 2026

He has spent his whole life being measured against European football's greatest goalscorer. Now Cristiano Ronaldo Jr. has taken his biggest step yet.

The 16-year-old has been called up to Portugal's U17 squad for the first time, and will face Andorra on November 11 and Serbia on November 14. And the timing is hard to ignore.

The famous No. 7 shirt Ronaldo Sr wore for two decades will now be vacant after he announced his retirement from international football on Thursday.

It's a heavy shirt for anyone to inherit. Luis Figo graced the number when he led Portugal’s golden generation to the 2006 World Cup semi-finals, and Ronaldo Sr himself carried it when he captained them to the European Championship in 2016. Both won the Ballon d’Or and are two of the most tantalising players the nation has ever produced.

Portugal’s power vacuum is also a pressure point. As the son of the man who wore that shirt, Ronaldo Jr. will attract more attention, and more expectation.

The national team lacks its vocal point, and few names carry more weight than his. He is the natural successor in marketing terms, if nothing else. Whether he is the player to take it is another matter.

Cristiano Ronaldo Jr - son of the Portuguese great - is looking to forge his own football career

This week the 16-year-old earned his first call-up to Portugal's U17 team

The weight of his father's expectations has been there from the start. Ronaldo Jr once floated the idea of becoming a goalkeeper, and his father’s reaction was swift. “No, I don’t want that! Are you joking or what?” Ronaldo Sr responds in the 2015 documentary Ronaldo.

Up front for the Juventus academy, his record would make the man chasing 1,000 career goals jealous: a staggering 58 goals in 23 games for the Under-9s. Yet his father was never satisfied. Asked at the 2020 Globe Soccer Awards, with his son sitting in the audience, whether the boy had what it takes to reach the top, Ronaldo Sr’s answer was blunt.

“Not yet,” he said. “I’m hard with him sometimes because he drinks Coca-Cola and Fanta. (He has) chips and fries; I fight with him.”

Hard data on his youth career since then is limited. Reports of his interest in switching to the Real Madrid academy suggested a desire to develop and compete.

Rio Ferdinand, who played alongside Ronaldo Sr. at Manchester United, has seen that competitive streak in the son on the padel court.

“I was in the Red Sea a couple of days ago; I play padel every day. (When) me and Cristiano Jr. get mad, we don't speak for like two days.” He exclaimed on Five Presents. Like his father, he doesn’t take losing well.

His body, though, has settled the question of position. At 6 ft 3 in, he already stands taller than his father. Growth spurts may temporarily cost him some of the pace and the effortless coordination of his youth. A forced adaption of his style is not unusual: Ronaldo’s former teammates Gareth Bale and Scott McTominay were both moved into new positions to begin their professional careers.

It is also a path his father walked. Forget stepovers, flicks and trademark ‘Ronaldo chop’. Jr’s game is currently closer to the Ronaldo of Juventus and the Old Trafford return: a penalty-box predator who lives on timing and movement rather than dribbling past defenders.

The young striker has represented the youth academies of Man United, Real Madrid and Juventus

But his ultra-professional father said his son needs to cut out the Coca-Cola if he wants to make it at the top level

His Portugal numbers are respectable, not remarkable. Five goals in 13 appearances is a decent return, but he has played just 522 minutes, an average of around 40 per game, and scored roughly once every 104 minutes. However, it is a tiny sample size.

To reach the top, he will need the work ethic his father is famous for. “I’ve never seen a more professional person,” Paul Scholes, Ronaldo Sr’s former Manchester United teammate, told Premier League Productions. “He was out there all day long, practising … he had weights on his ankles.”

Habits like that are built in demanding environments, and Jr’s has been a gentle one.

Playing in Saudi Arabia still has its positives. As Jr. transitions from boy to man, weaker opposition has given him room to grow into his body and build confidence as he prepares for men's senior football. But that breathing space has a shelf life.

He has options. He could stay and share a dressing room with his father, or return to one of the academies of Ronaldo Sr’s former clubs, with Real Madrid, Juventus and Manchester United all reported by The Sun to be interested. He has the name, the call-up and the options, but not yet the proof.

When Ronaldo Sr walked away from Portugal, he left behind a shirt, a record and a question. Saudi Arabia cannot give his son the answer. If he wants international caps and Champions League football, he must leave Al Nassr and his old man for a stage where nobody gives him an inch.

The surname opened the door. Only he can walk through it.

#1131. Manchester United stun Roma with three-goal second-half Champions League comeback after dreadful start

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

If this feels like vindication for Manchester United, it shouldn't. The sort of unforgettable European night you could have been forgiven for thinking might be a long time in coming for this listing club, certainly. A fresh start to a season that seemed on the brink, perhaps. And yet everything else does not go out of the window just because this team made Old Trafford roar again in a thrilling comeback to beat Roma 3-2.

A modicum of the commitment, energy and application they showed in the second half and United would never have been in the hole they found themselves in in the first. It turned out that when United do not just throw in the towel on the concession of a goal, there's still a decent football team lurking in there. More significantly than that, there are players who are still committed to the cause and perhaps to the manager. It surprised many that Michael Carrick got the backing of those above him after the defeat to Bournemouth nine days ago. This was as clear an indication as any that his players share his commitment to the cause, the belief he articulated on Monday.

Carrick might, however, ask where exactly this had been on the many occasions adversity came United's way in the last month. Why has everyone not been playing with the ferocity that Matheus Cunha used to carry this team back from the brink? The Brazilian was so exceptional you could forgive the overexuberance of a late red card. It was the same quality that saw him force the penalty through which the petulant Bruno Fernandes halved the deficit. The equalizer was afforded to Cunha when Leonardo Balerdi cleared fresh air. The winner only required a helping hand from Shea Lacey, Cunha taking the ball to a narrow angle and rocketing in a goal that seemed unimaginable when the hosts were being booed to the dressing room at the interval.

Old Trafford had been electrified. It hadn't taken much, that penalty where Fernandes was lucky to get a second chance after a questionable encroachment call. When Bryan Mbeumo clipped both posts, it sounded like the wobbly roof might come off. All it had taken was a few minutes of intensity and a browbeaten crowd roared again. Hope can now spring at a ground that really wants to believe that Carrick can get this right.

And yet whether he can will remain in doubt when so many of his players can fail to execute a game plan for so long, as they did in defeat at Como last month. That much was apparent for Roma's first goal. It was evidently part of Carrick's tactical plan to get Diogo Dalot high up the field early in the move to apply pressure to the right wing back. Risky, given the threat Matias Soule posed at the other end, but a perfectly valid approach. What would be required is some willingness on the part of others to plug gaps if Roma turned the ball over at the right moment.

Make no mistake, Dalot, stood with gray shirts between him and the ball, was not really making himself available for the pass. When Roma turned the ball over, however, the left back did blitz it back into position. There was just no way for him to get back in time. For Fernandes, perhaps there were gaps he could plug. Kobbie Mainoo too could have got in position. Instead, the right half of the penalty area was wide open for Soule to collect a pass from Rodrigo Mora and drive past Senne Lammens.

This is the sort of goal that, once you have conceded once, you ought never to again. Strictly speaking, United didn't; it is just that the penalty they conceded five minutes later again came because no one was filling the space vacated by Dalot. This time Soule tried to turn provider before getting the ball back off a lackadaisical Harry Maguire clearance. His shot deflected off Ayden Heaven's arm, Donyell Malen doubling the lead from the penalty spot.

The 28 minutes that followed were perhaps even more troubling. The legends of this football club are forged in fighting spirit on European nights, and yet defeat seemed to be accepted. United did not manage to take a shot in the penalty area in the first half. Amad Diallo seemed to be the only man who could get the ball into those dangerous areas. Meanwhile Fernandes carped at Carlos Baleba over a pass he didn't like. Baleba gave it back too. United looked to be on the brink.

It speaks favorably of Carrick that he turned it around not through any obvious tactical adjustments but through getting his side to move the ball with a little more intensity. They delivered it, and at the club that Sir Alex Ferguson built, there will always be a belief that a manager can come back from the brink to reach footballing immortality.

And yet the common thread of recent weeks is not that United can be as good as they were in the second half but that they can consistently plumb the depths they hit in the first. It only takes Morgan Rogers running in a straight line, Nico Paz finding space or Leny Yoro slipping to begin a chain reaction of mental anguish. On the evidence of tonight, those momentary crises were never intractable. Doesn't that make it all the more infuriating that United players were the first to call it quits?

#1129. Brighton underline title credentials with impressive win over Man City

This Brighton and Hove Albion title challenge – as it must now be classed – flies in the face of the saying that money always talks in football. Manchester City have been found guilty of breaching financial rules and also fielded the most expensive midfield in Premier League history here, yet the match-winners cost a fraction in comparison.

Looking at Brighton’s winning goal, it was created by a cross that flashed across the City goal from Diego Gómez, an £11m signing who was playing in Major League Soccer in the United States not so long ago. Maxim de Cuyper, a £17.5m arrival from Club Brugge, was credited with the assist after Yasin Ayari tapped in.

Ayari cost £3.5m from Swedish club AIK and scored in the 5-0 wins over Coventry and Palace, and now has this winner to add to his collection. The 23-year-old is another example of Brighton polishing these gems and putting them together in a team that can win against any opponent in the Premier League.

It could keep them at the top end of the table for a good while longer. They have already shown they can defeat Arsenal in a one-off match and they look to have the ingredients to stay the pace with them. In Fabian Hürzeler they have one of the brightest young coaches in the Premier League and he has a squad that are all on the same page.

Leicester upset the odds 10 years ago with a settled team, while this Brighton team has a deeper squad. When the substitutes came on in the second half, they slotted into a well-rehearsed system.

“We faced adversity. There was a little bit of luck but in the end they deserved it because they worked hard for it,” said Hürzeler. “I want players who want to compete, to dominate. They all have the winning mentality inside of them. These kinds of performances are not about one or two players, everyone has to stick together.”

See more of the month’s sharpest science shots, selected by Nature’s photo team.

An outbreak of anthrax has killed at least 30 hippos (Hippopotamus amphibius) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in the past month. No cases of the infectious disease have been reported in people so far. The wildlife outbreak puts further pressure on already limited resources, say researchers, as the DRC grapples with armed conflict and large outbreaks of Ebola and cholera.

Contributions to a United Nations-run pot for the conservation of nature — expected to raise US$1 billion per year — total just US$10,588 two years after it was established. The Cali Fund seeks voluntary contributions from companies that profit from genetic data collected from Earth’s biodiversity. So far, only five small biotech companies have contributed.

In the 2026 fiscal year, which ended on 30 September, the US National Science Foundation (NSF) funded fewer than 100 new social-science grants, compared with a historical average of roughly 850 per year. In dozens of programme areas, including economics and archaeology, the agency awarded no new grants at all. Earlier this year, the administration of President Donald Trump stated that it wants to eliminate the NSF’s social, behavioural and economic sciences (SBE) directorate altogether, leaving several decades-long projects hanging in the balance.

A study in mice might help explain the long-known fact that castration extends life span in most mammals, including people — and why men tend to live shorter lives than women. In the experiment, researchers removed the testicles of mice before puberty, after puberty or in old age, and found that all interventions increased median lifespan — with the late intervention leading to the biggest improvement. The findings suggest that testes’ apparently harmful effects begin later in life, rather than during their puberty heyday.

Widespread migration of people from countryside to cities is leading to a surprising drop in biodiversity in some of the low-intensity farming landscapes where humans have lived in harmony with other creatures for millennia. For example, in Japan, forests where farmers once cut trees for fuel and removed fallen leaves for fertilizer are becoming dense and closed in again — leading to losses in species such as fireflies and harvest mice. Volunteers have taken up saws to help, but experts say that longer-term solutions are needed, such as rewilding or addressing rural depopulation.

When Edward Freytag, a 66-year-old music teacher, injured his brain in a motorcycle crash, he developed the ability to instantly recognize musical notes. He’s the first person known to have acquired perfect pitch from a brain injury. In this beautifully illustrated feature, explore how our brains process sound, learn how Freytag’s injury might have affected him this way, and listen to a composition he wrote in a fugue-like state during the early stages of his recovery.

#1123. Barcelona's road back to the top runs through Lamine Yamal and Raphinha, and Aston Villa got a front row seat

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There are normal ways to build up to a marquee UEFA Champions League match and there's Aston Villa, for whom the top searches under Google's news tab were all about being taken seriously. This was hardly an exercise in projecting confidence ahead of a trip to Barcelona; the club picked a fight with a broadcaster instead because, for some reason, they deemed he had the power "to stop our ascension in English and European football." Villa's year-over-year improvements are hard to deny, to the point that being somewhat competitive at the Camp Nou on Tuesday was not out of the question and they managed that much. There was just one problem, though.

Punching above your weight is easier said than done against this version of Barcelona.

Villa were no slouch but over the course of a 3-0 win on Matchday 4 of the Champions League, Barcelona were simply in cruise control. It is not that Villa did not pose a challenge – they sparked at times in the first half, Johan Manzambi responsible for the visitors' best chance of the game around the half-hour mark. There was simply nothing they could do at the Camp Nou, their ascension irrelevant even if it is true, because Barcelona are as close to the summit as it gets.

Barcelona barely put a foot wrong as they strung together a trademark performance, well-positioned to do the easy things when the time called for them. That was true as soon as the seventh minute when Joao Gomes, under very little pressure, played a perfect pass to Lamine Yamal with plenty of space in front of him. Even as a couple of Villa defenders tried to close the space near goal, Yamal found his crevice and finished the chance off. It was perhaps the easiest way for him to score his 14th Champions League goal, surpassing Kylian Mbappe as the teenager with the most goals in the competition.

Lamine stands alone 😤Yamal scores his 14th #UCL goal to become the competition’s all-time leading teenage goalscorer 👏Watch #UCL on @paramountplus 📺 pic.twitter.com/Va8Ks3SEHv

The hosts overwhelmed Villa's defense with ease, Yamal's goal merely the first sign of trouble for the visitors. Raphinha bagged a 12-minute brace in the second half, the entire collection of goals a remarkable example of defensive errors. There's a comedy to the Brazil international's first goal, something casual about his strike despite three Villa defenders in his vicinity, watching the ball as it flew into the back of the net. On his second, Joao Cancelo was essentially given permission to dance around Villa's defense to find a Raphinha that was virtually unmarked and converted again from close range.

Raphinha with a 12-minute brace 💥He has scored 19 goals for Barcelona this season in all competitions 💥 pic.twitter.com/R39J7g9y6M

The mistakes from Villa were glaring, almost obfuscating Barcelona's performance entirely. It was not simply a walk in the park, though – Hansi Flick's side got to roll out Plan A and showcase its strengths fully, the lopsided result reflecting the more subtle elements of their dominance. They were able to possess exactly as they wanted to, taking 16 shots and generating 1.99 expected goals along the way. Their attacking might is hardly a surprise now that Raphinha is several years into a career revitalization steered by Flick and now that Yamal is already well known as the sport's next great talent.

What was more impressive was their ability to completely shut Villa out, especially so considering the circumstances. The game state was not exactly a deterrent to Unai Emery's side – 10 days earlier, they let Manchester City have the ball and took their chances despite posting 0.61 expected goals and notched a 2-1 win in the process. Their total was a little better on Tuesday at Barcelona, generating 0.72 expected goals from nine shots, and this time they had the benefit of playing against an understaffed defense. A series of injuries have plagued Barcelona's back line in recent weeks, stripping a defense of the early season stability that had become a new trademark despite sticking true to the high line.

Villa, though, were unable to make much of a dent. Nicolas Jackson, who had eight goals in 12 games across all competitions before the trip to Barcelona, took just one shot on Tuesday. Any semblance of attacking threat never came through. Rodri was not exactly some great denier, either – the captain of Spain's World Cup-winning team only played the first 45 minutes, earning the right to exit the game early after another job well done. Barcelona ensured Villa were dull over the course of 90 minutes; the defensive mistakes from the visitors were the end product rather than the cause of the hosts' success.

On a day where Villa's ascension was cast aside, Barcelona's rise was hard to miss. The gap they are trying to make up is smaller and easier to envision but it does not mean that Flick's side does not carry a certain amount of baggage on each and every Champions League night. They are 11 years removed from the last time they won Europe's top title, a lengthy stretch for one of the game's most celebrated teams. Self-imposed financial hardship has hindered their progress but since Flick took the job two years ago, they have inched closer and closer to the winner's medals they have been eager to collect.

Beating Paris Saint-Germain, the undeniable favorites after back-to-back titles, to the podium is another question entirely, especially after a 4-2 loss in the French capital on Matchday 3. Flick, though, insisted that day was merely a step on the journey, an experience to learn from as they attempt to ascend up Europe's ranks themselves. Champions often make their case on difficult days and should Barcelona make a deep run, they will likely have the chance to do just that down the stretch. The road to the Champions League title, though, usually includes some impressively unfussy days and on Tuesday, Flick's side collected one.

#1120. Viking's UCL journey and the rise of co-head coaches: Why two managers might be better than one

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Are two coaches better than one? This is a question that teams around the world, like Viking FK, are trying to answer as they bring dual head coaches to the big stage in Champions League play. The Norwegian side aren't alone in their exploits, as Lyngby in Denmark and Lincoln City in the English Championship are a few of the clubs to join in employing dual head coaches, but they're among the most notable, as Morten Jensen and Bjarte Lunde Aarsheim were able to lead the club to a 3-3 draw with Bayern Munich in Champions League play. There may just be a method to the madness.

Viking were trailblazers on the pitch, appointing the duo in 2020, and they helped lead the club to their first Norwegian league title in 34 years, which sent them into the Champions League for this campaign. Jensen and Aarsheim had chances to interview for the role, but being good friends off the pitch, they suggested taking it on together, a situation that the club has no regrets about as they add to the improving stature of Norwegian soccer.

"When the former coach left us, we knew we needed another coach, and we started the interview process. We brought the two assistant coaches in for different interviews, and then when the interview came, they just showed up together," club CEO Eirik Bjorno said, reminiscing on how this came to be to CBS Sports Golazo in September. "It was their idea. We said we needed to pick one of you, and they said that they were going to do it together. At the end, we said, 'Let's do it.' It has been fairly successful so far; there is no difference between them. They are both head coaches. It's fascinating when we have discussions: I discuss one thing with one of them, and then another thing with the other one, and then we sit down all together to find a solution. I just created more work for myself; I don't recommend it, to be honest."

But while they took a route of forcing the club's hand due to their own relationship and wanting to work together, that's not the only way for this to come to be. At Lyngby, the club wanted to install a dual setup when their manager, Morten Karlsen, was fired in December of 2025. Andreas Bjelland was already at the club as an assistant but had never held a head coaching role. When Mikkel Jespersen was recently let go from Mainz, the club reached out. As Jespersen described it, "We talked about life, football, everything just to see if there was a connection, and luckily there was, and we took it from there step by step, and we jumped into the cooperation."

Bjelland echoes how important it was for those meetings to go well before they jumped into managing Lyngby.

"Because you have to work really closely, it also has to be a person that you work quite well with and can understand and talk to in all kinds of different matters in life," Bjelland said. "So the meetings leading up to the co-coaching were the thing that gave the right feeling."

The duo may not be breaking down the door for the Champions League yet, but their leadership led the club to promotion back to the Danish Superliga, Denmark's top flight, while they're also helping shape the future of American soccer, as USMNT international Neil Pierre was part of the promotion-winning setup and Diego Kochen is currently the starting keeper for the club while on loan from Barcelona. The club hasn't won the Superliga since the 1991-92 season, so their path mirrors an early stage of Viking's, where the immediate goal is steady improvement in order to establish themselves back in the top flight, and the teamwork that Jespersen and Bjelland bring to the club makes them well positioned to do so.

"We're quite different. I think that's one of the things as well that really makes a good team, is that as persons we're quite different and how we act in front of the players, our personalities and all that stuff," Bjelland says. "A little bit like a relationship that you have to be different than your partner, else it wouldn't work. And that's for me a little bit the same, even though we don't hug and kiss. We still have to know a lot about each other, but being different is also a big thing about it that gives us all the tools that we have, so that we can cover more."

Differences in management are what bring a major challenge to balancing these roles. Bjorno spoke about needing to meet with both coaches about the same topics at Viking, and they've also opened up about how they need to work through disagreements when it comes to coaching decisions. You can't go out to the squad with one coach wanting to go in one direction while the other wants to go in the opposite, and that level of conflict resolution is something that these clubs go through behind closed doors ahead of time.

"Then we'll discuss, loudly sometimes, with the rest of our staff in the coaching room, and we will both have to defend our choices and reasoning to them," Jensen said in an interview with the Guardian. "We'll all discuss it until we have an agreement. But 99% of the time, we are pretty agreed in terms of who to use in a particular game, so it's very seldom we waste time over that."

Aarsheim added, "I can read Morten in one second. If he really wants something from his stomach, then I sense it: 'OK, let's go with that.' It's never been a problem."

It's similar at Lyngby, where the coaches have created a structure between themselves.

"We need to be really aligned in everything we do, and then the roles have to be really clear," Bjelland said. "So every day we know exactly who's doing what. So Mikkel has a lot of the things against the ball on minus three, and then I would have on the ball minus two. So everything we do is really structured. Of course, we discuss everything, and it takes some extra talks, and it takes some extra work to do, so we have to be pretty aligned in everything that we say and do."

The trust to know that a coach is saying what you'd expect when meeting with players is something that's built through working together, and when done well, it can make the job easier for those involved because you have someone to brainstorm with and work on tactical decisions with. In life, it's natural to have someone who can be a sounding board, and while assistant coaches can do that too, it's a different power dynamic than when someone is in the same position as you as a head coach.

"Yeah, it is. Especially when it's the first time both of us are head coaches," Jespersen said on the comfort of having a dual manager in charge with him. "It's nice to have each other to talk everything through. Also, when you're in doubt, it's nice to have someone who maybe has the same doubts as you to make the right decision."

It takes a particular style of group to make it work, but these clubs are using it with success, and it could be something that others try to emulate. Watching Viking perform and manage this at the highest level, others have already followed, with Lyngby and Lincoln City moving in the dual head coach direction in the past year. If that continues to catch on,  we may be seeing the buds of a new coaching revolution in the global game.

#1118. Spurs win three in row for first time in 616 days to pile pressure on Sage

For the first time in 616 days, Tottenham Hotspur have won three Premier League matches in a row. Three different managers have been sacked in that time, and the mood in north London had plunged to grim lows, but finally there is a sense that something truly exciting is stirring at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

This victory over Crystal Palace was not as impressive as last week’s triumph at Chelsea, but it did not need to be. After Palace striker Jean-Philippe Mateta was sent off in the 13th minute, Spurs simply had to make their numerical advantage count. They did so with relative ease, taking complete control of possession and creating endless goalscoring opportunities.

Roberto De Zerbi’s team ended the night with 34 shots to Palace’s two and with 758 completed passes to Palace’s 149. The goals ultimately came from two defenders, Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke, but there was a long list of Spurs players who might have scored here.

Spurs take the lead through an Archie Gray header! ⚪ https://t.co/qSCECkOJur

Did this defeat mark the end for Pierre Sage, the Palace manager? The Frenchman was only appointed in June but it has been a grisly start to the campaign. Palace have the worst defence in the league, have lost six of nine games and have not produced any truly encouraging performances in the Premier League.

Even in the two games Palace have won, against Fulham and Nottingham Forest, they were lucky to do so. The likes of Sean Dyche and Thomas Frank, both of whom would be strong candidates to replace Sage if Palace do pull the trigger, will no doubt have been keeping an eye on events here.

“I am really aware of the situation,” Sage said. “I don’t like this situation. [But] you can trust in me, I will never give up. I want to be the first on the pitch on Monday. I have the rage to train more. It’s not me to decide this thing [his future]. If I have one hour, I will give my best for one hour. If I have 10 years, I will give my best for 10 years.”

The decision for Palace chairman Steve Parish, then, is whether this result represented a continuation of the team’s problems or was an aberration caused by the early red card. It would be reasonable for Sage to claim this match was out of his hands from the moment Mateta lunged at Spurs captain Micky van de Ven, but such an argument might not carry much weight with Palace sitting 18th in the table.

The challenge was foolish in the extreme by Mateta, a player who was much more successful in exiting this game than he has been in his numerous attempts to leave Palace in recent transfer windows. At first glance it did not seem the worst tackle, but the replays were damning: Mateta led with his studs and made forceful contact with Van de Ven’s ankle.

It was an inexcusably brainless act, after just 13 minutes of play, and the same could be said of Palace’s defending from a right-wing corner a few minutes later. Mohammed Kudus swirled the delivery to the back post, where Gray was unmarked. Yes, Palace were defending with 10. But no, that does not justify the inability of Sage’s players to spot Gray. Even more embarrassingly, the Tottenham player was unmarked again from another corner shortly afterwards.

It was not the first time this season that Palace’s cause has been undermined by a red card. When they lost at home to Ipswich Town in September, Axel Disasi was sent off after 34 minutes. An absence of discipline? Perhaps. Sage might argue, though, that he is not responsible for his players demonstrating a lack of basic brainpower.

All of this was welcomed heartily by the Spurs fans, who celebrated Mateta’s dismissal as though it was a goal. Recent results have restored some of the enthusiasm in this corner of north London and the mood here was buoyant, even before Gray’s opener.

“Now we are playing as a team,” De Zerbi said. “Before the international break, we were playing as many good players but not as a team. We showed our maturity. We are improving.”

The second goal was always coming and it arrived in the 73rd minute, when Van Hecke attacked a wonderful cross by Mateus Fernandes. Palace goalkeeper Dean Henderson saved the first attempt but the ball dropped onto the head of Van Hecke, now seated in the six-yard box, and he happily nodded it home.

The new signings at Spurs endured a difficult first few weeks but there were more signs here that they are adjusting to De Zerbi’s system. Spurs face Leeds United, Ipswich Town, Sunderland and Fulham in their next four league games. The momentum could, and perhaps should, continue to build. Their optimism here contrasted sharply with the angst of Palace, and with the troubled look that was etched on Sage’s face.

“Very pleased for the performance, very tough game. You don’t know 11 [against 11] would be different game but Crystal Palace are very tough because they defend with a low block, no space and we showed we are a mature team. When asked if Spurs are looking up the table, he replied: “We don’t forget the ambitions. We have to look behind what was the situation two weeks ago. In the last two years, two times 17th in the table, many games without a win in front of our fans. We have to stay focused. They are improving, increasing the level of performance.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Palace defender said: “Definitely was frustrating. It was one of the first tackles of the game. And we felt like we were doing well and it is unfortunate. We go again.
